materials.title: The Last Tray
materials.text:
At Westbridge College, students used to gather outside the campus bakery just before closing. They hoped to buy the remaining bread at half price. Some arrived so early that they waited through their afternoon classes. Meanwhile, staff could not tell how many people would come. On rainy days, unsold rolls sometimes went into the waste bin despite the discount.

The bakery manager, Elena Shaw, proposed an online reservation service. Each afternoon, customers could order a bag containing three items. They would collect it during the final twenty minutes of business. The bag cost less than choosing three items separately, but customers could not select its contents. Shaw thought advance reservations would help staff prepare bags and reduce the uncomfortable queue outside.

The first week brought a surprise. Staff received many reservations, yet there was less bread left than expected. To fill the bags, a baker made an extra tray of rolls. The bakery had sold more food, but its waste project had become an ordinary sales promotion. Shaw stopped accepting reservations before the afternoon stock count. Now, staff first counted the bread that was actually left and then released only that number of bags online.

Students raised a different concern. The college offered no evening bus from the science buildings, and some laboratory classes ended after the collection window. A cheap bag was of little use to students who could not reach it. The student union asked for delivery across campus. Shaw rejected that idea because the small bakery had no driver. Instead, she agreed that one student could collect bags for several classmates, provided the order numbers were shown.

There was also an information problem. One customer opened a bag and discovered a cheese pastry she could not eat. Although the reservation page had listed common ingredients, the list was too general to identify every item. Staff began attaching the original product labels to each bag. Customers with food allergies were advised to buy individually labelled items at the regular counter, where they could check the exact contents before paying.

After six weeks, the bakery compared its records with those from a similar teaching period. Fewer items had been thrown away, and the late queue had nearly disappeared. However, Shaw refused to describe every reserved bag as food saved from the bin. Some customers would have bought the same bread at full price. The records could show a reduction in waste, but they could not reveal what each shopper would otherwise have done.

The student union kept the project and changed its publicity. The poster now promised discounted remaining bread, rather than a guaranteed environmental benefit from every purchase. For Shaw, this modest claim was a sign that the experiment had improved. A useful service did not need a larger story than the evidence could support.

questions.prompt: Why did the bakery originally have difficulty managing its discounted bread?
options: Staff were required to close before students finished classes.
The number of late customers was uncertain.
Students refused to buy bread on campus.
The college prevented staff from changing prices.
questions.explanation: B正确：首段说员工无法判断会来多少人，雨天仍有剩余。A把部分学生下课晚扩大成全部且非原始困难；C与排队购买相反；D文中没有禁止改价。

questions.prompt: What was a condition of buying a reserved bag?
options: Customers had to purchase a drink as well.
Customers could choose any three products.
Customers had to join the student union.
Customers accepted the items chosen for the bag.
questions.explanation: D正确：第二段明说不能选择袋中内容。A没有饮料要求；B与不能选内容矛盾；C没有学生会会员条件。

questions.prompt: Why did Shaw change the time when reservations became available?
options: The bakery needed to sell only bread already remaining.
The website could operate only after classes.
Staff wanted to bake a special range for online customers.
The original price was lower than the cost of flour.
questions.explanation: A正确：先盘点再放出相应袋数，避免为了填预订而额外烤面包。B没有网站时段限制；C正是被纠正的额外生产方向；D没有面粉成本信息。

questions.prompt: What does “an ordinary sales promotion” suggest in paragraph 3?
options: A campaign that prevented all food purchases.
A rule that applied only to bakery employees.
A project that had lost its original focus on existing surplus.
A method that eliminated the need for any stock count.
questions.explanation: C正确：额外烤一盘使原本处理余量的项目变成促进销售。A与卖得更多相反；B不是员工规则；D随后恰恰增加先盘点的步骤。

questions.prompt: How did the bakery respond to students with late laboratory classes?
options: It allowed one person to collect several classmates’ orders.
It moved all classes to the main campus.
It kept the counter open throughout the night.
It provided a free evening delivery van.
questions.explanation: A正确：第四段允许凭订单号代同学领取。D送货因无司机被拒；B面包房未调整课程；C没有通宵营业。

questions.prompt: Why were original product labels attached to the bags?
options: To advertise a new supplier of cheese.
To give more specific information about individual products.
To allow customers to select the contents online.
To prove that every item had been baked that morning.
questions.explanation: B正确：通用配料清单不足以识别每项食品，原标签提供具体信息。A无新供应商；C内容仍不可选；D标签措施并非为了证明烘烤时间。

questions.prompt: Which customer is specifically advised to use the regular counter?
options: A student collecting several order numbers.
A customer wishing to avoid the late queue.
A student seeking any discounted remaining bread.
A customer needing to check food allergens before payment.
questions.explanation: D正确：有食物过敏者应在付款前核对单独标签和确切内容。A代取可用预订；B预订本就减少晚间队列；C无需因此去常规柜台。

questions.prompt: What limitation did Shaw identify in the six-week records?
options: They covered only a period when the college was closed.
They recorded orders but omitted all discarded items.
They did not show what each customer would have bought without the scheme.
They proved that the new system increased waste.
questions.explanation: C正确：记录不能揭示每位顾客在没有项目时的选择。B记录用于比较丢弃量，非全数漏记；A为相似教学时段；D观察到丢弃更少。

questions.prompt: How did the student union revise its publicity?
options: It announced that discounted bags would soon be banned.
It described the concrete offer without guaranteeing a benefit for every purchase.
It claimed the project had removed the need to bake fresh bread.
It promised a personal environmental score for each shopper.
questions.explanation: B正确：海报只承诺折价余量面包，不再保证每笔购买都有环保收益。A没有停办；D没有个人分数；C仍有正常烘烤业务。

questions.prompt: Which statement best expresses the passage’s main idea?
options: A surplus-food service improved by adjusting its rules and limiting its claims.
Discounting food always creates more waste than it prevents.
Online sales are unsuitable for every small campus business.
Students should take responsibility for running all college shops.
questions.explanation: A正确：全文依次呈现余量、领取和信息问题的调整，最后强调宣传应受证据约束。B与废弃减少冲突且绝对化；C把具体可改进问题变成全面否定；D没有让学生接管商店的主张。

materials.title: A Line Everyone Could Read
materials.text:
When the sports department of Alder Town planned to repaint its public tennis courts, it invited residents to suggest improvements. Most replies concerned brighter lamps or longer opening hours. One message, however, came from a local group of older players. They explained that the pale court lines were difficult to see against the faded green surface, especially in the late afternoon.

The department first tested a much brighter white paint on one court. In photographs, the result looked excellent. Yet several players still had trouble following the ball near the far baseline. The problem became clear when maintenance officer Jay Patel watched a game instead of examining another photograph. Sunlight reflected from the glossy paint directly towards the players at one end. A brighter line could also become a source of glare.

Patel asked the painting contractor to prepare three small test areas outside the playing surface. All used the same white colour, but their finishes differed. Volunteers walked past them at several times of day. A finish that reflected less light received the strongest support. The department then used it on the test court, leaving the other court unchanged until players had tried both.

The trial also revealed a disagreement about markings. A youth coach wanted extra lines for a smaller training court, so beginners could practise on a space suited to their reach. Regular adult players worried that another set of lines would make matches confusing. The department did not settle the matter by counting the two groups’ emails. The coach had sent one message on behalf of twenty children, while individual adult players had each written separately.

Instead, the department arranged two open sessions. During the first, beginners used temporary coloured tape for the smaller court. During the second, adult players tried ordinary matches with the tape still in place. The coach discovered that one crossing line distracted even some children. He shortened that section of tape, and the next session ran more smoothly. The final plan included a few short training marks near the edges rather than a complete second rectangle.

Some residents asked whether the changes had made the courts safer. Patel was careful with his answer. Players reported that the lines were easier to follow, but the trial had not measured injuries. In addition, the trial took place in dry weather. The new surface still needed inspection after rain before officials could make claims about wet-weather use.

The department published the final design beside a short account of the rejected ideas. This included the glossy paint, which had looked so convincing in the first photographs. Patel hoped future projects would begin with people performing the actual activity in the actual place. A picture could show where a line was, he said, without showing whether someone could comfortably play a game beside it.

questions.prompt: What specific difficulty did the older players report?
options: The booking website would not accept their names.
The nets were too high for afternoon matches.
The court lines were hard to distinguish from the surface.
The courts closed before sunset every day.
questions.explanation: C正确：首段指出浅色边线与褪色绿色地面难辨。A无订场问题；B未提网高；D“每天日落前关闭”无依据。

questions.prompt: Why did the first bright paint fail to solve the problem fully?
options: Its glossy finish reflected sunlight towards some players.
It disappeared completely after one game.
It changed the height at which the ball bounced.
It could be seen only in photographs taken at night.
questions.explanation: A正确：第二段现场观察发现光泽涂料向一端球员反光。B没有脱落；C未谈球弹跳；D照片并非仅夜间可见。

questions.prompt: What remained the same in the three small paint tests?
options: The single afternoon time chosen for all inspections.
The white colour used for the samples.
The opinions of all the volunteers.
The amount of light reflected by each finish.
questions.explanation: B正确：三处都是同样白色而表面处理不同。A声称只选一个下午时间，但志愿者在多个时段查看；C仅说某处理支持最多，并非意见全同；D反射差异正是试验变量。

questions.prompt: Why was the second court initially left unchanged?
options: It was reserved permanently for professional competitions.
Its users had refused to join any public discussion.
The contractor had run out of every kind of paint.
Players needed to be able to compare the two courts.
questions.explanation: D正确：一场改造、一场保留，等球员都试用后比较。A无职业赛事专用；B无拒绝参与；C无缺漆。

questions.prompt: Why would simply counting emails misrepresent the views about training lines?
options: Only children were allowed to send messages.
One coach’s email represented a group, while adults wrote individually.
All adult messages had been copied from the coach.
The department had accidentally deleted the children’s replies.
questions.explanation: B正确：教练一封代表二十个孩子，成人逐人发送，邮件数不等于人数。A与成人发信矛盾；C没说抄袭；D无删除事件。

questions.prompt: What does “settle the matter” in paragraph 4 mean?
options: Make the court surface completely flat.
Arrange a financial payment to the coach.
Resolve the disagreement over the markings.
Move all games to another town.
questions.explanation: C正确：matter指训练线之争，settle为解决争议。A是球场施工义而非语境；B没有付款；D没有异地搬迁。

questions.prompt: What caused the coach to revise his initial arrangement?
options: A crossing line distracted some of the beginner players.
The temporary tape was impossible to remove.
All adult players refused to try the taped court.
The children asked for a larger professional court.
questions.explanation: A正确：开放试用发现交叉线也分散孩子注意，于是缩短。B未说胶带不可去除；C成人进行了第二场试用；D孩子没有要求更大场地。

questions.prompt: Which claim was supported by the trial as described?
options: The new paint prevented all injuries.
Players found the lines easier to follow.
Extra training marks helped every player equally.
The courts performed better in heavy rain.
questions.explanation: B正确：球员报告边线更容易跟随。A未测伤害且“全部防止”绝对化；D只在干燥天气试用；C没有“每人同样受益”的结果。

questions.prompt: Why did the department publish rejected ideas?
options: To prevent residents from offering further suggestions.
To show that the first photographs were digitally altered.
To blame older players for the cost of repainting.
To explain how practical testing shaped the final design.
questions.explanation: D正确：被否方案与过程同发，展示实际试用如何影响成案。A与鼓励实际参与的结尾不合；C没有归责；B照片好看不等于被篡改。

questions.prompt: What broader lesson does Patel draw?
options: All photographs are useless in planning public facilities.
The loudest group should decide which facilities are built.
Design should be tested through real use in its intended setting.
Sports departments should avoid trying unfamiliar materials.
questions.explanation: C正确：末段强调人在真实地点从事真实活动。A把照片局限扩大为全无用；B邮件计数的讨论恰不支持此意；D试用不同材料促成改进。

materials.title: After the Garden Gate Closed
materials.text:
Visitors to the Linden Community Garden usually noticed the bees first. They moved between the flowers while children watered vegetable beds nearby. The garden’s annual report listed daytime insect sightings, and the committee used those records when choosing plants. Flowers that attracted few visible visitors were often replaced the following spring.

One volunteer, Ruth Ellis, questioned what the list left out. She worked in the evening and often reached the garden just before its gate closed. On warm nights, she had seen moths hovering around a white flowering plant that seemed almost ignored during the day. She suggested a short night survey before the committee removed that plant. Her aim was not to prove that moths were more important than bees, but to discover who else used the garden.

The committee approved four evening visits. Volunteers did not leave the gate open to the public, because the garden’s insurance covered supervised activities only. Instead, a small registered group entered with the caretaker. They stood beside selected plants and recorded insects for ten minutes at each location. Phone screens were turned down, and a shielded lamp lit the path rather than the flowers.

The first visit produced few sightings. Some volunteers thought the night survey had failed. Ellis pointed out that a cold wind had risen during the hour before sunset. On the second visit, when the evening was warmer and calmer, the same plants received several moth visitors. The group therefore added weather notes to its record sheet. They did not compare two evenings as though the conditions were identical.

Identifying the insects was another challenge. In a dim photograph, two kinds of moth could look much alike. A local naturalist reviewed the images and asked the volunteers to leave uncertain entries at the broader category of “moth”. Several people disliked losing detailed names from their lists. The naturalist replied that a less specific record could be more useful than an exact name attached to the wrong insect.

By the end of the four visits, the white flowering plant had several confirmed moth observations. The committee decided to keep a small patch for another season. It also retained popular daytime flowers, since the new observations did not make the bee records irrelevant. Rather than choose a single winning plant, the gardeners wanted flowers available to different visitors at different hours.

The night survey did not establish the total number of moths living in the neighbourhood. Volunteers had watched only selected plants for short periods. Its value lay in exposing a gap in the garden’s usual routine. The next annual report placed day and evening observations in separate columns, with dates and weather beside them. A reader could now see both the new visitors and the limits of the effort that had found them.

questions.prompt: How had the garden usually chosen which flowers to replace?
options: By using records that mainly covered daytime insects.
By asking children to vote for their favourite colours.
By comparing prices at nearby supermarkets.
By measuring every plant’s growth during winter.
questions.explanation: A正确：首段说白天昆虫观察记录影响选花，少见访客的花常被替换。C无超市价格；B孩子只在浇水，未投票；D没有冬季生长测量。

questions.prompt: Why did Ellis propose a night survey?
options: She believed all white flowers should be removed.
She wanted the garden to stop recording bees.
She suspected that the existing records missed some plant visitors.
She intended to open the garden all night for tourists.
questions.explanation: C正确：她黄昏见到蛾，想知道还有谁使用花园。B文中明确不是证明蛾比蜂重要；A她要在移除前调查；D并非通宵开放。

questions.prompt: Why was the evening group registered and accompanied by the caretaker?
options: The naturalist could identify insects only in small groups.
The flowers could survive only when few people were present.
The volunteers were collecting plants for a private sale.
The insurance covered supervised activities rather than unrestricted access.
questions.explanation: D正确：第三段以保险只覆盖有监督活动解释入园安排。A未提自然学家人数限制；B花卉生存条件无此说；C无售卖采集。

questions.prompt: How did the volunteers use the lamp?
options: They shone it directly into every flower.
They lit the path while shielding the light from the flowers.
They used it to warm insects on cold evenings.
They kept it off while opening the gate to everyone.
questions.explanation: B正确：有遮罩灯照路而不是照花。A与原文相反；C无加热用途；D夜间并不全面开放。

questions.prompt: What did the contrast between the first two visits lead the group to do?
options: Cancel the remaining survey visits.
Conclude that moths never visit in windy weather.
Record weather conditions alongside observations.
Replace all of the chosen observation plants.
questions.explanation: C正确：冷热、风况不同促使表格加入天气。A四次继续完成；B个别观察不能推出“从不”；D没有更换观察植物。

questions.prompt: Why did the naturalist recommend the broad label “moth” for some entries?
options: Every moth in the garden belonged to the same species.
The volunteers had photographed only butterflies.
Specific moth names were forbidden in the annual report.
A cautious general identification was preferable to a precise error.
questions.explanation: D正确：专家认为不够具体但可靠的记录胜过精确错名。B没有全是蝴蝶；C无禁用物种名规定；A两类难辨不等于同一种。

questions.prompt: What does “retained” in paragraph 6 mean?
options: Continued to keep.
Covered with a new label.
Moved to a distant park.
Sold to raise money.
questions.explanation: A正确：委员会保留夜间植物同时继续保有受欢迎的日间花卉。D无出售；B非重新贴标；C无迁移。

questions.prompt: Which planting decision followed the survey?
options: Replace daytime flowers with a single kind of night flower.
Stop growing all flowers that attracted bees.
Keep a small patch of the white plant as well as daytime favourites.
Remove the white plant because the first visit found little.
questions.explanation: C正确：第六段保留一小片白花，并留日间花。A、B把互补选择改成全替换；D忽略后续确认蛾访客和保留决定。

questions.prompt: Why could the survey not establish the neighbourhood’s total moth population?
options: The report did not contain a separate column for evenings.
Observation covered selected plants and short periods only.
The naturalist refused to review any photographs.
No insects were seen on any of the four visits.
questions.explanation: B正确：末段明确样本地点及观察时长有限。A新报告有独立晚间栏；C专家已审图；D后续有多次确认观察。

questions.prompt: Which title best captures the central message?
options: A Change in Observation Reveals an Overlooked Part of a Garden
Why Bees No Longer Belong in Community Gardens
A Complete Count of Every Insect in Linden
How to Identify All Moths from a Single Photograph
questions.explanation: A正确：夜间观察补上惯常白天记录盲点，且明确限度。B无排斥蜜蜂；C不是完整普查；D辨认困难恰反对此说。

units.alignmentNote: Existing frozen original supplies level and four-option reading task rules only. All passage prose, questions, keys and explanations in this draft are newly authored; this is not an official CET paper or independently calibrated material.

materials.title: Two Colours of the Same Cloth
materials.text:
The oldest object in Harbour Textile Museum’s new display was a small piece of blue cloth. It had once covered a shop window, where sunlight fell on it for years. By the time the museum received it, one side had faded almost to grey. The other side, protected by the window frame, still held a deep blue strip along its edge.

Curator Mina Cole wanted visitors to understand both colours. The pale area recorded what had happened to the cloth, but the surviving edge suggested how it might originally have looked. Simply calling the object “blue cloth” would hide its present appearance. Calling it “grey cloth” would erase evidence of its earlier life. Cole decided that the display should let people compare the two without pretending that the museum could return the original to its first condition.

A technician proposed projecting blue light onto the faded area. The test looked impressive from the doorway. Up close, however, the added light made it harder to examine the worn threads. It also affected nearby objects. Cole abandoned the projection and asked for a separate digital image beside the case. Visitors could press a button to switch between a photograph of the cloth today and an estimated version of its earlier colour.

That word “estimated” mattered. The protected strip offered a useful clue, but the cloth might not have been perfectly uniform when it was new. The team therefore avoided the label “the true original colour”. On the screen, a short note explained which part of the object had guided the reconstruction and which details remained uncertain. A printed photograph of the current object remained visible even when the screen was switched to the earlier version.

During a trial, visitors spent more time pressing the button than reading the note. Some left believing that museum staff had physically dyed the cloth blue again. To correct this, the team changed the screen’s opening sentence to “This image changes; the cloth in the case does not.” They also placed the button beside the screen instead of on the case. In the second trial, fewer visitors confused the digital image with treatment of the object.

The display included a second, modern piece of fabric that visitors could touch. This sample had a similar weave, but Cole refused to describe it as an exact copy. Its fibres and production process differed from those of the historical cloth. The sample helped visitors feel a woven surface; it could not tell them precisely how the older material had felt in someone’s hand.

For Cole, the finished display was successful because it made several kinds of evidence visible. Visitors could inspect the aged object, explore a possible earlier appearance, and touch a related material. Each offered something useful, and each had a clear limit. The museum’s task was to make those limits understandable while leaving room for curiosity.

questions.prompt: Why had a strip of cloth kept a deeper blue colour?
options: The museum had recently painted it.
Visitors had been forbidden to photograph it.
It was woven from a different material.
It had been protected by the window frame.
questions.explanation: D正确：首段说明窗框保护的边缘保有深蓝。A原物未重新上色；C没有材料不同；B无摄影禁令。

questions.prompt: What difficulty did Cole see in naming the object’s colour?
options: The cloth had never had a visible colour.
Neither “blue” nor “grey” alone explained its history and present state.
The museum could not print colour labels.
The shop owner had asked the museum to conceal its colour.
questions.explanation: B正确：蓝色单称会遮蔽现在外观，灰色单称会抹去早期证据。A明显有颜色；C无印刷困难；D无店主要求。

questions.prompt: Why was the blue-light projection rejected?
options: It could not be seen from the doorway.
It revealed that the cloth was a modern copy.
It interfered with examining the cloth and affected other objects.
It permanently changed every thread to blue.
questions.explanation: C正确：近看难辨磨损纱线且影响邻近展品。B无真假发现；A从门口看很出色；D投光未永久染色。

questions.prompt: What could visitors do with the digital display?
options: Switch between its current photograph and an estimated earlier appearance.
Order an exact copy of the cloth.
Adjust the colour of every nearby exhibit.
Choose which original threads to remove.
questions.explanation: A正确：按钮切换现状照片和估计的早期色彩图。D无拆线权限；B无订购；C数字屏不改变展品颜色。

questions.prompt: Why did the museum avoid calling the reconstruction “the true original colour”?
options: The protected strip contained no useful information.
The team had decided to ignore the cloth’s earlier life.
The digital screen could show only black and white.
The original cloth might not have had one perfectly uniform colour.
questions.explanation: D正确：边条虽有线索，但新布可能不完全均匀，因此不能断言唯一真色。A与有用线索相反；C屏幕展示色彩；B重建正用于探索早期外观。

questions.prompt: What misunderstanding appeared during the first visitor trial?
options: Some visitors believed that the actual cloth had been dyed again.
Visitors assumed the museum had closed its textile collection.
Visitors thought the screen was a photograph of another museum.
Some visitors believed that touching historical fabric was compulsory.
questions.explanation: A正确：第五段说明有人误认为工作人员已给实物重新染蓝。C、B无此误解；D触摸对象是现代样品且无强制。

questions.prompt: How did the team try to make the digital reconstruction’s status clearer?
options: It stopped visitors from using the button.
It removed every current photograph from the room.
It explicitly said that the image changed while the object did not.
It placed the screen inside the cloth’s original window frame.
questions.explanation: C正确：改开场句“图像变化，柜中实物不变”，并调整按钮位置。B仍有印刷现状照；A继续按钮交互；D没有此摆放方式。

questions.prompt: What does “weave” mean in the description of the modern sample?
options: The shop where an item was sold.
The pattern formed by interlacing threads.
The number of years an object was displayed.
The chemical used to remove a colour.
questions.explanation: B正确：织物和woven surface语境中weave为纱线交织结构。A是商店；D是染整化学品而非结构；C是年代，与similar weave不合。

questions.prompt: What could the touchable sample reasonably show?
options: A related example of a woven surface.
The exact feel of the historical cloth when new.
The amount of sunlight the old cloth had received.
The original shop owner’s preferred colour.
questions.explanation: A正确：现代样品帮助感受相关编织表面，不能精确复现旧物手感。B被明确否定；C不能触摸推出光照量；D无店主偏好证据。

questions.prompt: How is the passage mainly organised?
options: It lists famous textile museums in date order.
It compares competing scientific theories of sunlight.
It argues that digital displays should replace historical objects.
It follows display choices and revisions that clarify different kinds of evidence.
questions.explanation: D正确：围绕命名、投影、数字说明和触摸样品的选择修订展开。A没有博物馆列表；B无理论论战；C实物始终是证据来源之一，非被取代。

units.title: 六级阅读：未达预期实验的公开记录
units.alignmentNote: Existing frozen original supplies level and four-option reading task rules only. All passage prose, questions, keys and explanations in this draft are newly authored; this is not an official CET paper or independently calibrated material.

materials.title: When a Result Does Not Travel
materials.text:
A research result can disappear without anyone destroying a document. It may remain in a laboratory notebook, discussed at one meeting and then omitted from the account that travels beyond the research group. This is particularly likely when an experiment fails to support its starting expectation. The difficulty is not merely that unsuccessful work receives less attention. When readers encounter only the successful attempts, they may develop a distorted picture of how reliably an approach works.

At the fictional Bellwater Institute, a group studying water filters established a register for trials that had not produced the expected improvement. The register was separate from the institute’s collection of published papers. A paper presented a sustained argument; an entry in the register described a particular test, its conditions and its outcome. The distinction allowed researchers to share a limited observation without pretending that every entry was a complete investigation suitable for a journal.

Early entries, however, exposed an ambiguity in the expression “did not work”. In one trial, a filter failed to remove the target substance. In another, it removed the substance but damaged the testing equipment. A third had ended before a valid measurement could be taken. These records could not all be treated as evidence that the underlying filter design was ineffective. The register therefore introduced separate fields for the intended outcome, the observed result and the reason the team considered the trial inconclusive or disappointing.

Some researchers worried that competitors would use the entries to judge their competence. The institute responded by allowing a short delay before public release, giving teams time to check technical details and prepare related papers. It did not permit an indefinite delay simply because a result looked unflattering. This compromise recognised that the practical interests of researchers affected whether the register would be used at all. Yet it also made those interests visible instead of disguising them as purely technical decisions.

The register’s managers resisted another apparently helpful change: ranking entries by how often their methods had subsequently succeeded elsewhere. A frequently repeated method might acquire a high score, while a specialised test could remain unranked for years. That score would reflect attention as well as reliability. It might also encourage readers to treat a result obtained under one set of conditions as a verdict on a method in every setting. Entries instead linked to later studies, leaving readers to examine how the conditions compared.

After a year, several teams reported that the register had saved them from repeating an unsuitable procedure. The institute welcomed these accounts but did not convert them into an estimate of total money saved. Teams that found an entry useless had little reason to report their experience, and there was no record of every project that might have proceeded without the register. The stories demonstrated possible uses; they could not establish the average benefit across all research.

The larger value of the project was a change in what could count as a contribution. An experiment no longer needed to become a triumphant narrative before another group could learn from it. That did not make a poorly documented result valuable automatically. On the contrary, publication of limited outcomes required unusually careful descriptions of limits. The register widened access to research experience by narrowing the claims attached to each record, offering readers grounds for judgement rather than a simple label of success or failure.

questions.prompt: What distortion does the opening paragraph identify?
options: Researchers are unable to remember any experiment that fails.
Laboratory notebooks routinely contain no record of successful work.
Readers may overestimate an approach’s reliability when only successes circulate.
Journal articles always report a higher measurement than the original data.
questions.explanation: C正确：只传播成功尝试会使读者误判方法有多可靠。A把记录未传播说成研究者完全遗忘；B文中没有常规不记成功的说法；D没有指控期刊总夸大测量值。

questions.prompt: How did an entry in the register differ from a published paper?
options: It contained a complete investigation but concealed all test conditions.
It described a bounded test rather than necessarily offering a sustained full argument.
It was accepted only after being rejected by several journals.
It was intended to replace the institute’s entire paper collection.
questions.explanation: B正确：第二段对照完整论证的论文与描述具体试验及条件结果的条目。A条件恰需公开；C无多次退稿要求；D登记册与论文库并存。

questions.prompt: Why are the three filter trials described in paragraph 3?
options: To show that equipment damage is always the main cause of failure.
To prove that all three filter designs should be abandoned.
To suggest that only completed trials deserve any documentation.
To illustrate why the label “did not work” needs to be unpacked.
questions.explanation: D正确：未去除、去除却损坏设备、未得有效测量是不同结果，不能一个失败标签概括。A只一例损坏；B不能都推为设计无效；C登记册仍记录未完成测量的局限。

questions.prompt: What was the purpose of permitting a short release delay?
options: To accommodate checking and related publication without allowing unlimited concealment.
To allow embarrassing results to remain permanently private.
To remove the need to check the entries’ technical details.
To guarantee that no competitor could ever read an entry.
questions.explanation: A正确：短延迟用于核对技术细节和相关论文，但不允许因难看而无限延期。D登记册最终公开；B与禁无限延期相反；C核对正是目的之一。

questions.prompt: What does “unflattering” most nearly mean in paragraph 4?
options: Difficult to convert into a digital format.
Unfavourable to the researchers’ reputation.
Too complicated for a specialised reader.
Unrelated to the filter under investigation.
questions.explanation: B正确：前文担心竞争者评价能力，因此unflattering指有损形象的结果。A无格式问题；C不等于复杂；D结果与研究相关。

questions.prompt: Why did the managers reject a ranking based on later successes?
options: Such a ranking could confuse how much attention a method received with how reliable it was.
The institute had lost access to all later studies.
Every registered method had already been tested equally often.
Researchers had agreed that methods could never be compared under any conditions.
questions.explanation: A正确：常被重复的方法分高，专门测试久无分，反映关注度也反映可靠性。C恰有不同重复机会；B仍链接后续研究；D不是禁止一切比较，而是需要比较条件。

questions.prompt: What did linking to later studies allow readers to do?
options: Avoid reading the conditions of the original experiment.
Assume that one successful replication settled all questions about a method.
Consider whether differences in conditions affected the relevance of later findings.
Infer that every linked study had been conducted by Bellwater researchers.
questions.explanation: C正确：第五段让读者核对试验条件如何可比。B正是作者警惕的跨情境总判决；A应查看而非跳过条件；D未限定后续研究机构。

questions.prompt: Why were reports of saved effort insufficient to estimate total savings?
options: The reports proved that no money was ever spent on repeated procedures.
Every research team had submitted an identical account.
The institute deliberately excluded all successful examples.
The reports were selective and lacked a record of all projects that might have used the register.
questions.explanation: D正确：无用者少报告，也没有所有潜在项目的记录，不能估计总体平均受益或总节省。A无此证明；B未说全员同报；C实际欢迎有用案例。

questions.prompt: What relationship does the final paragraph establish between openness and precision?
options: Sharing limited outcomes can be useful when claims and limitations are carefully specified.
Wider access removes the obligation to document uncertain outcomes.
Every unsuccessful experiment becomes useful as soon as it is made public.
Public registers should contain only claims that apply to every research setting.
questions.explanation: A正确：扩大经验可及性，同时收窄每条记录主张并细述局限。B与需特别谨慎相反；C作者明确否认自动有价值；D不要求普遍适用，强调限定情境。

questions.prompt: Which description best captures the author’s overall position?
options: Unsuccessful experiments are generally more trustworthy than successful ones.
Researchers should stop writing full papers and publish only test records.
A register can reveal overlooked experience, provided it preserves distinctions and restrained claims.
The chief value of research records lies in ranking competing laboratories.
questions.explanation: C正确：全文支持公开被忽略的经验，同时区分结果、条件和证据范围。A无成功失败可信度排行；B论文和条目功能互补；D排名甚至被拒绝。

units.title: 六级阅读：居家照护排班中的连续性
units.alignmentNote: Existing frozen original supplies level and four-option reading task rules only. All passage prose, questions, keys and explanations in this draft are newly authored; this is not an official CET paper or independently calibrated material.

materials.title: The Minutes Between Visits
materials.text:
For a home-care worker, a timetable is also a map of obligations. It determines how long a worker can remain with a person who needs help dressing, whether a delayed bus will affect the next visit, and how often a client must explain a familiar routine to a stranger. A schedule can therefore become more efficient by one measure while making the service less dependable by another. The question is which consequences the scheduling system is instructed to notice.

The fictional North Quay care service introduced software intended to reduce travel between appointments. Its first comparison looked encouraging: the distance travelled per completed visit fell. Managers had previously arranged routes largely within fixed neighbourhood teams; the software treated the whole district as a single pool. It found shorter journeys by assigning whichever available worker was nearest to a client, sometimes replacing a familiar worker who was travelling from farther away.

Clients’ complaints revealed what the distance measure omitted. A woman with limited speech relied on a particular sequence of gestures to indicate how she wished to be helped. A new worker could learn the sequence, but repeated changes meant repeatedly teaching it. The software counted a completed visit whether the interaction went smoothly or required a long explanation. Continuity had practical value even where it could not easily be expressed as a number of kilometres.

The service responded by requiring the system to prefer a small, familiar set of workers for each client. Managers described this as adding a human consideration to an otherwise neutral calculation. A workers’ representative challenged the wording. The original calculation had already embodied a judgement: that shorter travel should take priority over familiar relationships. Adding continuity did not introduce values into a value-free process. It altered the balance between values that had been there from the start.

A further problem emerged when managers examined late arrivals. The software used average journey times, which concealed large variation on one bus route. On most mornings the trip was quick; occasionally a missed connection produced a substantial delay. Adding the same buffer to every journey would have lengthened the whole working day. Instead, schedulers reserved more flexible time around the unreliable connection and allowed workers to flag unusual delays without immediately being marked as personally responsible.

The changes improved the schedule in the service’s next review, but an easy comparison remained elusive. During the same period, one difficult route acquired a more frequent bus service, and the agency took on clients with different needs. The managers could document fewer reported changes of worker and fewer recorded late arrivals. They could not confidently assign every improvement to the revised software. In particular, counting complaints alone would have been hazardous, since clients differed in how comfortable they felt raising concerns.

North Quay retained the software, with regular meetings at which workers and clients could challenge its assumptions. No meeting could settle the competing demands permanently: staff availability, individual preferences and transport conditions would change. The point of review was to keep decisions open to correction. Workers also needed time within their paid day to attend these discussions; otherwise participation would favour those able to donate time, and the review process could reproduce a different form of inequality. A timetable became accountable when those affected could question why it allocated their time as it did, rather than merely receive a finished answer whose priorities were hidden inside a seemingly objective route.

questions.prompt: What central problem is introduced in the first paragraph?
options: Care workers cannot use public transport during working hours.
A schedule’s apparent efficiency depends on which effects are measured.
Clients generally prefer a different worker on every visit.
Every care visit requires exactly the same amount of time.
questions.explanation: B正确：一个指标效率提高可能使另一个指标的可靠性下降，关键在系统注意哪些后果。A无公交禁令；C与后文连续性需求相反；D需求不同，并非等时。

questions.prompt: How did the original software reduce travel distance?
options: It cancelled every appointment outside a worker’s home neighbourhood.
It required clients to travel to a central care facility.
It replaced all bus journeys with private-car journeys.
It selected nearby available workers across the whole district.
questions.explanation: D正确：第二段把全区作为人力池选最近可用人员。A并未取消跨区预约；B仍是上门服务；C无车辆全面替换。

questions.prompt: What does the example of the woman with limited speech demonstrate?
options: Repeatedly changing workers can impose an uncounted burden on the client.
A completed visit always guarantees a satisfactory interaction.
Gestures prevent any unfamiliar worker from ever providing care.
Travel distance is the only reasonable way to measure care quality.
questions.explanation: A正确：反复教手势增加负担，完成次数不反映互动成本。B正是计数遗漏；C新工人可以学会，不是永远不能；D例子揭示距离指标不足。

questions.prompt: Why did the workers’ representative object to the word “neutral”?
options: The program had never calculated travel distance accurately.
The service was legally forbidden to consider efficiency.
The original system already prioritised one value over another.
Familiarity could be measured only by software.
questions.explanation: C正确：优先短路程本身是价值判断，并非无价值中立计算。A没有计算失准的证据；B未说禁止效率；D没有软件独占测量说法。

questions.prompt: What does “embodied” most nearly mean in paragraph 4?
options: Accidentally concealed from every manager.
Copied word for word from a client’s letter.
Corrected by removing all assumptions.
Expressed or gave practical form to.
questions.explanation: D正确：原计算把短路程优先的判断落实于实际安排，embodied意为体现。A不必然为意外隐藏；C没有消除所有假设；B没有信件原文。

questions.prompt: Why were average journey times inadequate for one bus route?
options: The route was slower than every other route on every morning.
The workers refused to report how long their journeys took.
Occasional severe delays were hidden by a generally quick journey.
The system had treated all journeys as journeys on foot.
questions.explanation: C正确：多数日快，偶尔错过换乘大幅迟延，平均值掩盖波动。A并非天天最慢；B可以报告异常，无拒报信息；D没有当作步行。

questions.prompt: How did schedulers address the unreliable connection?
options: They added an identical large buffer to every journey in the district.
They placed extra flexibility around that connection and let workers report unusual delays.
They made every worker personally responsible for missed bus connections.
They stopped serving every client reached by that route.
questions.explanation: B正确：对不可靠换乘安排更灵活时段并允许标记异常延误。A是被避开的全面延长方案；C无需马上个人归责；D没有停止服务。

questions.prompt: Why could managers not attribute all improvements to the software revision?
options: Transport provision and the mix of clients had also changed.
The revision was never used for real appointments.
The clients had all moved out of the district.
The service had stopped collecting arrival records.
questions.explanation: A正确：同期公交更密、客户需求不同，存在其他变化。D仍有到达记录；B已实施后复核；C没有全体搬走。

questions.prompt: Why would complaint counts alone be a hazardous basis for evaluation?
options: All complaints were generated automatically by the scheduling program.
The service was required to ignore spoken complaints.
Clients differed in their willingness to express concerns.
A low complaint count necessarily proved that continuity was poor.
questions.explanation: C正确：不同客户提出意见的自在程度不同，少投诉不能直接等同好服务。A无自动生成；B无忽略口头投诉规则；D也不能反向必然证明差。

questions.prompt: What does the final paragraph suggest makes the timetable accountable?
options: A permanent rule that no worker or client can question.
A guarantee that all competing needs will disappear.
A calculation that gives travel distance exclusive priority forever.
A continuing opportunity for affected people to examine and challenge its priorities.
questions.explanation: D正确：相关人能询问时间为何如此分配并持续纠偏。A与开放纠正相反；B需求会变、竞争无法永久解决；C距离独占恰是要审查的优先次序。

units.title: 六级阅读：潮汐湿地修复的碳账本
units.alignmentNote: Existing frozen original supplies level and four-option reading task rules only. All passage prose, questions, keys and explanations in this draft are newly authored; this is not an official CET paper or independently calibrated material.

materials.title: Where the Carbon Account Ends
materials.text:
A restored marsh may look like a straightforward environmental success. Water returns to ground once drained for farming, plants spread, and birds begin to feed along the channels. Turning that visible transformation into a carbon account is less straightforward. The account must compare what happens after restoration with a plausible description of what would have happened without it. Neither a photograph of new vegetation nor a measurement taken on one afternoon can supply that comparison alone.

In a fictional coastal district, planners proposed reopening a barrier so that tides could enter abandoned fields. Their initial carbon estimate counted the carbon expected to accumulate in the new marsh soil. An adviser asked what would happen to the site if the barrier remained closed. The fields were no longer being cultivated, but drainage pumps still operated. If the pumps would have continued running, their energy use belonged in the comparison. If they were already scheduled to stop for another reason, crediting the restoration with that entire saving would exaggerate its effect.

The same concern applied beyond the site boundary. A local landholder suggested that the restored area’s former crop production should be treated as permanently removed. Yet the fields had produced no crop for several years. Conversely, if an actively farmed site were restored and its production moved elsewhere, some consequences might appear outside the project map. A neat boundary was useful for administration; it did not guarantee that all relevant environmental changes occurred inside it.

These questions did not imply that restoration should wait until every consequence was known. They indicated which assumptions had to accompany an estimate. The planning team produced several scenarios rather than a single unexplained number. One assumed continued pumping without restoration; another assumed that pumping would soon cease anyway. The scenarios gave decision-makers a range and showed why it existed. They were not alternative measurements of the same future waiting to be averaged.

Timing introduced a further complication. New vegetation could establish quickly, whereas changes in soil carbon might unfold over a much longer period. The project also required fuel for construction work at the barrier. Reporting only the eventual accumulation would obscure the immediate cost; reporting only the construction emissions would obscure the continuing process. The team therefore presented a time profile, indicating early emissions and later expected gains, with uncertainty increasing farther into the future.

Public discussion nevertheless focused on whether the scheme could be called “carbon positive” at its opening ceremony. Some residents found the refusal to give a simple answer evasive. The adviser argued that the label compressed several questions into one: positive over what period, compared with which alternative, and including which effects? A qualified estimate could support a decision more honestly than a confident label whose boundaries no one had examined. The team also listed benefits such as habitat restoration separately, so these were neither erased by uncertainty about carbon nor used to inflate the carbon figure.

The proposal ultimately went forward with monitoring requirements and a published account of its assumptions. Its approval did not establish that every predicted gain would occur. It established that the planners considered the expected benefits sufficient under stated conditions. Future measurements could then test the estimate and inform revisions. The carbon account became a tool for learning and comparison because its boundaries were available for inspection, rather than hidden behind the apparent precision of a final total.

questions.prompt: What essential comparison does the opening paragraph say a carbon account requires?
options: The number of birds at the site and at every neighbouring farm.
The appearance of the marsh at dawn and at sunset.
The size of the opening ceremony and the construction workforce.
The effects of restoration and a plausible future without it.
questions.explanation: D正确：需比较修复后的结果与未修复时合理的反事实路径。A鸟数不足以构成碳比较；B只比较外观时段；C仪式与人数无关。

questions.prompt: When would crediting the project with all savings from stopped pumps exaggerate its effect?
options: When pump electricity use was included explicitly in a scenario.
When the fields would otherwise have continued to require pumping.
When the pumps were going to stop for an independent reason anyway.
When the restoration allowed tidal water to enter the fields.
questions.explanation: C正确：若泵本就因别的原因计划停止，其全部节能不能归功修复。B继续抽水恰是可纳入基准的情况；A明确纳入不必然夸大；D进潮本身不能判定节能归因。

questions.prompt: Why was the local landholder’s claim about removed crop production questioned?
options: The project promised to expand crop production inside the new marsh.
The fields had already stopped producing crops years earlier.
The planners had forbidden any discussion of agriculture.
The landholder had mistaken the district’s location.
questions.explanation: B正确：闲置数年，无现有产量可简单宣称永久减少。A没有新湿地增产计划；D无地点误认；C农业影响正在讨论，非禁止。

questions.prompt: What does the discussion of production moving elsewhere illustrate?
options: Administrative boundaries may exclude consequences relevant to an environmental account.
Environmental changes always stop at a project’s legal boundary.
Restoring any field necessarily increases farming emissions elsewhere.
All effects outside the project map can be measured without assumptions.
questions.explanation: A正确：若活跃农地产量转移，后果可能在图外，行政边界不包尽相关影响。B与此相反；C原文是条件情形而非所有项目必然；D仍需假设而非无假设测量。

questions.prompt: Why did the team present several scenarios?
options: To let decision-makers select whichever number appeared most impressive.
To postpone any decision until all futures became certain.
To show how different baseline assumptions changed the estimate.
To obtain a single forecast by mechanically averaging incompatible futures.
questions.explanation: C正确：不同是否继续抽水的假设形成范围并说明来源。A不是挑好看数字；B明确不应等一切已知；D原文明说不是等待平均的同一未来测量值。

questions.prompt: What does “obscure” mean in paragraph 5?
options: Calculate with complete accuracy.
Make less visible or harder to understand.
Remove permanently from the physical site.
Describe in chronological detail.
questions.explanation: B正确：仅报长期积累会遮蔽早期成本，反之亦然，obscure为使难以看清。A精确计算相反；C账目遗漏并非物理消除；D时间细述是后续解决方法。

questions.prompt: What information did the time profile preserve?
options: Only the construction workforce’s annual pay.
Only the carbon gain expected at the most distant date.
A guarantee that uncertainty would disappear after the ceremony.
Both early emissions and the expected accumulation over later periods.
questions.explanation: D正确：时间图展示早期施工排放与后期预期积累，远期更不确定。A无工资；B不是只取最远收益；C不确定性没有随仪式消失。

questions.prompt: Why did the adviser resist the simple label “carbon positive”?
options: The label concealed choices about timescale, comparison and included effects.
The adviser believed no restored marsh could ever store carbon.
The public had requested that carbon be excluded from the discussion.
The team had already measured every future effect with certainty.
questions.explanation: A正确：标签压缩“多长期间、对比何种替代、包含何种效应”多项问题。B没有否认储碳可能；C公众正关注碳；D远期有不确定性。

questions.prompt: Why were habitat benefits listed separately from the carbon estimate?
options: To suggest that birds could be counted directly as carbon units.
To recognise these benefits without converting them into unsupported carbon gains.
To remove habitat protection from the approval decision.
To prove that habitat benefits must always exceed climate benefits.
questions.explanation: B正确：独列使栖息地收益既不被碳不确定性抹去，也不被拿来增碳数字。A非碳单位；C仍是收益之一；D没有必然大小排序。

questions.prompt: What did approval of the proposal actually establish, according to the passage?
options: Monitoring was no longer needed once a number had been published.
Every projected carbon gain had already occurred before work began.
The expected benefits were judged sufficient under explicit conditions, with predictions still open to checking.
The initial estimate would remain correct regardless of later measurements.
questions.explanation: C正确：批准是既定条件下认为预期收益足够，并非预测必成，后续监测可修订。B收益尚属未来；A要求监测；D未来测量可纠正估计。

units.title: 六级阅读：仪式面具数字档案的访问权限
units.alignmentNote: Existing frozen original supplies level and four-option reading task rules only. All passage prose, questions, keys and explanations in this draft are newly authored; this is not an official CET paper or independently calibrated material.

materials.title: A File Is Not the Whole Return
materials.text:
When a museum sends a high-resolution scan of an object to the community from which it came, the transfer can be described as a form of digital return. The phrase sounds reassuring: a distant object has become locally available, and many people can inspect details that were previously difficult to see. Yet availability is only one dimension of return. A file can arrive with restrictions, descriptions and technical dependencies that leave important decisions in the hands of the institution that sent it.

In a fictional collaboration, the Estuary Museum worked with a coastal community to scan a ceremonial mask held in its collection. The museum’s digital team initially proposed placing the model in a public online catalogue. Their usual policy treated unrestricted viewing as the most generous arrangement. Community representatives explained that the mask was traditionally viewed only in certain settings. Publishing a freely rotatable model would make some details visible in ways that an ordinary encounter with the object never did.

The disagreement was not resolved by asking whether the community supported technology. Several representatives wanted local students to study the model and wanted craftspeople to examine its construction. What they disputed was the assumption that a museum’s preference for maximum access should decide every use. The partners eventually agreed on different levels of access: a public description, a limited set of approved images, and a detailed model available through a community-managed process.

Description presented a related problem. The catalogue had long identified the mask by a collector’s short label and a broad regional category. Neither was simply erased, because both helped document how the museum had acquired and classified the object. But the new record placed the community’s preferred name and account first, while explaining where the older labels came from. The result preserved evidence of earlier institutional practice without allowing that practice to remain the only voice describing the mask.

Technical arrangements then tested how substantial the transfer really was. The first copy could be opened only through the museum’s paid viewing platform. If the subscription ended, local users would retain data they could not conveniently inspect. The museum supplied an additional version in a documented format, along with instructions for exporting and maintaining it. This did not guarantee permanent access: equipment and software would still need attention. It did reduce dependence on one institution’s continuing contract with a commercial provider.

Some museum staff worried that multiple descriptions and changing access permissions would make the catalogue inconsistent. The project coordinator distinguished inconsistency from recorded disagreement. A catalogue could explain who made a statement, when a permission changed, and which uses were authorised, rather than force every contribution into a single unchanging account. Maintaining such a record required work. Calling the initial upload a completed return would conceal the continuing responsibility to manage relationships as well as files.

The collaboration did not settle the separate question of whether the physical mask should remain in the museum. A digital model could support teaching and discussion, but it was not treated as a substitute for resolving ownership. The project’s achievement was more limited and more concrete: the community gained a greater role in naming, accessing and maintaining a representation of its heritage. The case suggests that digital return should be judged by the distribution of practical authority after a transfer, rather than by the impressive size or visual detail of the file alone.

questions.prompt: What assumption does the first paragraph question?

Communities can inspect a digital object in detail.
All digital files are smaller than physical objects.
A transferred file may require technical support.
